claims.text: The initial HEA is a homogeneous single-phase FCC or BCC solid solution with a uniform elemental distribution.
The initial HEA exhibits ductile failure under conventional quasi-static loading.
The initial HEA has higher fracture toughness than it will have after demanding mechanical loading.
High-magnitude or cyclic mechanical loading causes localized compositional heterogeneities to develop in the initially homogeneous HEA.
Localized elemental enrichment originates at sites of high dislocation accumulation and stress concentration.
High or cyclic loading produces evolving dislocation interactions and strain localization.
Dislocation interactions and strain localization induce local atomic rearrangements and compositional fluctuations.
Load-induced compositional fluctuations nucleate incipient brittle secondary phases.
The incipient secondary phases provide preferential sites for crack initiation.
The load-induced microstructural changes impair crack blunting or arrest.
The load-induced secondary phases reduce fracture toughness and promote brittle failure.
Severely loaded samples will have lower crack-initiation toughness or K_Ic than the baseline samples.
Severely loaded samples will show cleavage or other brittle fracture morphologies rather than ductile dimples.
The proposed behavior applies when cyclic stresses or overloads push the alloy into nonlinear deformation and local stress concentrations can trigger phase instability.
The loading threshold and extent of phase separation depend on alloy composition and test parameters.
A controlled comparison should expose otherwise identical samples to severe cyclic or high-magnitude loading and benign quasi-static loading.
Testing should be performed near or above yield at service-relevant amplitudes, frequencies, and temperatures while environment and specimen geometry are controlled.

The hypothesis is falsified if loaded samples show neither a statistically significant toughness reduction nor detectable localized phase separation or brittle secondary-phase formation relative to controls.
